segments.text: Hey friends, 18-year-old Rahul was sitting in his college canteen talking
to his friend.
Suddenly, his friend said something that left him shocked.
His friend shared that he had started investing in the
stock market because his father had motivated him to do so.
In fact, his father told him that if he starts investing in the stock market from
today, by the time he reaches his father’s age, he could have crores of rupees.
After hearing this, Rahul burst out laughing.
He said, “You? A millionaire?
You don’t even have money to eat in the canteen, and you’re
talking about becoming rich!” He brushed it off as a joke.
But maybe that day, Google or YouTube’s algorithm caught his words.
From that day on, he kept seeing different videos and content related to the
stock market again and again.\ He started seeing reels and posts
everywhere about how people were investing in different stocks and making money.
Watching all these videos again and again slowly sparked curiosity inside him.
He didn’t know anything about the stock market, so he decided that he would
go and take some advice from his uncle who invests in the stock market.
Now, Mr.
Mehta was known
as the “stock market uncle” because he had been investing for the past 15–20 years.
Many times, he had lost a lot of money, and many times, he had made a lot as well.
Basically, he had a great deal of experience.
So Rahul went straight to him and told him how his friend had started investing,
and that he was also thinking about starting his investment journey.
In the share market… As soon as the uncle heard Rahul say this, he became quite
interested and, smiling, asked, “Rahul, do you know what a
stock or a share actually is?” Rahul’s face looked a little confused.
He kind of knew, but at the same time, he didn’t really know much.
So the uncle decided to explain with an example.
He said, “Look at the pizza kept in front of you.” Now imagine
this is a pizza worth ₹500, but you don’t have ₹500 — you only have ₹100.
Since this pizza belongs to me, I can cut it into five equal slices.
If I want, I can give you one slice in exchange for ₹100.
That slice would basically represent 20% of the pizza.
Now replace this pizza with a company.
The slice you get after paying ₹100 becomes one share out
of five —
in other words, 20%
ownership of the company.
Now, usually companies don’t have just five or ten shares.
Many times, a company has millions of shares.
But overall, the concept remains the same.
After hearing
this, Rahul understood a little, but he still seemed slightly confused.
So the uncle gave another example.
“Suppose, Rahul, you want to open a café, and the total investment required is…”
₹5 lakhs.
But you only have ₹1 lakh.
Now you know someone who is also planning to start a business, and he has ₹4 lakhs.
You have ₹1 lakh, he has ₹4 lakhs.
Together, you can invest ₹5 lakhs and open a café.
Now, for easy understanding, let’s assume
that this café is divided into 100 shares.
Since you invested ₹1 lakh out of
₹5 lakhs, you would own 20 shares of the café — which means 20% ownership.
That means you would become a 20% owner of the café.
After hearing this, Rahul finally understood the concept a little better.
But as soon as he understood it, another question popped into his mind.
He asked, “Uncle, okay, I understand this part.
But why would anyone sell their company?
And that too to someone like me?
Why would they make me an owner of their company just because I have 20%?”
“I would also kind of become an owner?” The uncle said, “Yes, exactly.”
He then explained, “Look, every company needs money to run and grow.
For example, if a person is running one café and wants to expand his business
by opening cafés in different locations, he will need more money to do that.”
To run his café, he needs raw materials, he has to hire staff, and there
are many other expenses involved in running and expanding a business.
Now, to manage these expenses, he has two main options.
Either he can take a loan from a bank, for which he will have to pay interest.
Or instead of paying interest, many people choose to raise money from
investors and make them partners.
This way, they don’t have to pay interest, and somewhere down the
line, having partners can also make it easier to run and grow the business.
At the initial stage, the people
from whom money is raised are often angel investors or VCs (venture capitalists).
But as the company grows bigger and starts selling its shares — parts
of the company — to the general public, that’s where an IPO comes in.
IPO stands for Initial Public Offering.
“Yes, I’ve heard about IPOs many times in the news,” Rahul said. “Yes.
That happens when a company is made public — when ordinary people can also buy a
share of that company through the stock market.” Rahul found this quite logical,
and for the first
time, he started understanding the concept of stocks a little better.
He then asked, “But how will investors make money?
Will they take money
from the company’s profits?” “Look, there are two ways to make money from shares.
First, take the café example I gave you.
Let’s say the total valuation of the café was ₹5 lakhs.
That means the whole business was worth ₹5 lakhs.
You bought 20% of the company.
Now suppose the café starts growing.
Its profits increase, demand rises, and the business becomes more successful.
Obviously, the value of that café — which was earlier just ₹5 lakhs — might now
become ₹10 lakhs.” Where you had bought 20% shares for ₹1,00,000, their value
would now become ₹2,00,000.
So you can sell your shares and make a profit.
That’s the first way. The second way is through dividends.
Sometimes companies give dividends to their shareholders.
This means if the café is earning very good profits and has excess cash, and
the owners don’t want to reinvest that cash
into the business, they may distribute a part of that profit to the shareholders.
That share of profit is called a dividend.
“Basically, you invested your money, and
that money started making more money.” Rahul
said, “Oh, so it’s like making money from money.” The uncle smiled and said, “Yes,
that’s the magic.” After that, the uncle drew a simple diagram on a piece of paper.
Rahul asked, “What is this?” He replied,
“This line you’re seeing represents compounding.
If you invest ₹1 lakh in a business and
it grows at 10% per year, this line won’t
remain straight over time.” Instead, it will form an exponential curve.
That means after some
time, your ₹1 lakh could even turn into ₹1 crore or ₹10 crores in 10–20 years.
But yes, it takes time.
And this is called compounding.
The moment Rahul heard “crores,” he became alert.
“If all this is so easy, then why doesn’t everyone become rich by investing
in the stock market?
It can’t be that simple.” Suppose you invested
₹5 lakhs in that café.
Initially, it was making
a monthly profit of ₹1 lakh.
As it grew, the monthly profit increased to ₹2 lakhs.
When the profit increased, the valuation
of the café went from ₹5 lakhs to ₹10 lakhs. But what if that doesn’t happen?
What if you invested ₹1 lakh in the café, and instead of earning a profit
of ₹1 lakh as expected, you only start earning ₹50,000 — or even less?
Then obviously, the value of your café will decrease because it
is not generating good profits.
That’s why it is very important to invest only in the right companies
— the ones you believe have long-term potential and can grow big in the future.
After hearing all this, Rahul felt a little confused and remained quiet.
He slowly asked his uncle, “Uncle, which companies should we trust in the market?”
The uncle asked him, “What kind of things do you use in your
daily life?” Rahul started thinking — Google, YouTube, Instagram, Zomato, Ola.
The uncle smiled and said, “Yes.
Peter Lynch, who is a legendary investor, says that the businesses you understand
and personally use can often give
you good results, because you already have some knowledge about them.”
“For example, you’ve been using Google for many years,” the uncle said.
Rahul replied, “Yes.” “Do you think in the next five years Google will grow
or collapse?” Rahul said, “I think it will grow.” “Then you can
consider investing in it — because behind
such companies there is strong leadership, a solid
balance sheet, global presence, and a strong business model.
It may not be perfect, but it has strong fundamentals.”
“It’s not risk-free either,” the uncle continued.
“But even if you
haven’t done deep research yet, you can still make a basic judgment that this
is likely a good company.” Rahul then asked, “But uncle, these companies are
foreign, not Indian. Should we invest in foreign companies too?
And what about companies in our own country — aren’t they profitable as well?”
The uncle found this question quite interesting.
He said, “Look, it’s not necessary to invest in foreign companies, but it can
be a smart decision.” Rahul asked, “How?” He replied, “For five reasons.
First, companies like Google are global giants.
With the AI revolution coming
in, companies like these are likely to stay ahead in many
of these areas.” In areas like cloud computing and semiconductors, these
are global tech leaders.
Companies like Google, Apple, Microsoft,
and Amazon don’t operate only in the US — they do business all over the world.
They even have a strong presence in India.
We use their products daily.
So instead of just contributing to their profits
as customers, why not start taking a share of their profits as investors?
Rahul smiled and nodded his head.
The uncle explained, “The second advantage is the dollar advantage.
When we invest in US stocks, somewhere we are investing in dollars.
Historically, we’ve seen
that the Indian rupee has often weakened against the dollar.
So if we invest
in dollar-based companies, directly or indirectly we are investing in dollars.
In a way, this also gives us currency diversification.” “Diversification?
What is that?” Rahul asked.
The uncle smiled and said, “I’m glad you asked,
because the third advantage is exactly diversification.
Warren Buffett, who is one of the greatest investors in the world, says,
‘Never put all your eggs in one basket.’ That means if you carry all your eggs
in one basket and that basket falls, all your eggs will break.” Similarly, if you
keep all your investments in just one market
or invest everything in a single company, the chances of risk increase.
Sometimes the Indian market goes down.
Sometimes the US market may also go down.
But that’s exactly why, if you diversify your money and invest across different
markets, you can achieve better stability in your overall portfolio.
“The fourth advantage is dividend and growth.
Many US companies regularly pay dividends.
They share a small portion
of their profits with shareholders, which can act as a form of passive income.
And lastly, fractional investing. Many foreign stocks are quite expensive.
Sometimes you may not have enough money
to buy one full share — some shares can cost ₹20,000 or ₹30,000 or even more.
But many international companies allow
fractional investing, which means you can buy a small part of a share.
This way, even with a small investment, you can own a small portion of a big
company.” “So, because of these five reasons, investing
in foreign companies can sometimes be a smart decision,” the uncle concluded.
Rahul then asked, “But uncle, how do we buy US stocks?
It must be very difficult, right?
There must be international accounts, taxes, currency
conversion and all that…” The uncle found his curiosity interesting and smiled.
“Yes, you’re right.
There was a time when international accounts,
taxes, currency conversion — all of this used to be quite complicated.”
“But now, many Indian platforms have come up.
Personally, I use one of them — IND money.
I really like some of its features.” Rahul asked, “Oh really?
What kind of features?” The uncle said,
“First of all, through this platform you can very easily start investing in the US.
You can directly buy US stocks.”
“There’s no need to do complex international paperwork.
You don’t have to open a difficult foreign account.
You simply follow the steps in the app, fill in the required details,
complete your KYC, and you can easily start the buying and selling process.
So the first thing is — it’s a simple app to use.
Second, as I mentioned earlier about fractional shares — just go and check what
the current share price of Google is.” Rahul checked and said, “It’s
315 dollars.” The uncle replied, “Basically, that means one share
is selling for around ₹29,000.
You probably don’t have ₹29,000 to invest directly right now, right?”
Rahul said, “Yes… but look, there’s an option
here for fractional shares.” The uncle nodded, “Exactly.
You can set a small amount and buy a fraction of the share.
That means even expensive stocks can be bought according to your budget.”
“The third good thing is that it offers a Stock SIP.
In India, people usually do SIPs in mutual funds.
But through this app, you can now do SIPs directly in stocks as well.
That means you can invest regularly in a particular
company to maintain discipline and benefit properly from compounding.
If you set up a system where ₹500 or ₹1,000
gets deducted automatically every month, then you are automatically
investing every month without having to think about it.”
“…without putting in your active time every month,” the uncle explained.
Rahul said, “Yes, that makes sense.” “The fourth benefit is dollar exposure.
Since the investment is US-based, it can act as a hedge against rupee depreciation.
And the fifth is smart tools.
In INDmoney, you can see a company’s performance, the
overall market mood, how much interest people are showing in US stocks,
how much trading is happening — all explained in simple language.
Based on sentiment analysis,
you can get an idea of how market emotions are moving.”
“Basically, it’s youth-friendly.
It’s useful for young people like you.
It’s visual and easy to understand — you can quickly see where the market
is going and what’s happening. You can also track dividends from here.
If you invest in dividend stocks, you can track your passive income easily.
So, I hope
from all this you’ve gained at least some knowledge?” Rahul replied, “Yes.”
The uncle then said, “If you
also want to start investing with INDmoney, I’ll share the link with you.”
“You can go there right now and start your investment journey,” the uncle said.
Rahul replied, “Okay, I’ll start investing right away.
I’m even thinking of taking some money from Dad and investing everything
— putting all my money into foreign stocks.” The uncle quickly stopped
him and said, “Wait. Look, it’s not that simple.
You should never invest all your money in just one place.”
“That’s the biggest mistake beginners make.
They think if they put all
their money in one place, it will double or triple and they’ll become rich.
It doesn’t work like that. You need to follow some rules.
There are four rules. The first rule — right now you’re young.
As you move forward, the very first thing you must build is an emergency fund.”
Before investing, you need to have safety.
That means you should have enough money set aside
so that if any emergency happens tomorrow, you have funds available to handle it.
The second rule is diversification.
Instead of putting all your money into
just one company or one market, it’s better to spread your investments
across different markets, different companies,
mutual funds, and various assets — and try to build a balanced portfolio overall.
Spread your risk.
Diversification may feel boring, and the returns might sometimes be slightly lower,
but the risk is also lower — and that’s what smart investing is all about.
So remember this rule.
Rule number three: Have a long-term mindset.
In the short term, even if you invest in a big company, the price can go down.
But over the long term — 5, 10, or 15 years —
it has often been seen that markets tend to give good returns.
“As you can see in this graph…” “Rule number four: Don’t follow flashy
tips or flashy influencers.
In fact, don’t even follow my advice blindly.
Whatever I’ve told you is based
on my experience — but my experience can also be wrong.
That’s why it’s important for you to do your own research and
decide which company you believe can give you the best returns.”
“Do as much analysis as you can.
Read and learn as much as possible before you start investing.” Rahul replied,
“Okay, I will start investing too — but only after doing my own research
and studying properly. Until then, I’ll begin with small investments.
I’ll put in only that much money which, even if I lose it, I
won’t feel stressed.” The uncle smiled and said, “Smart boy,” and then he left.
Now listen, friends — if you’re also a young person who wants to start investing,
you can do it through INDmoney.
The link is in the description.
When young people start investing and stay invested for the long
term, three things work in their favor: time, compounding, and ownership.
This is a very powerful combination.
It won’t make you rich overnight, but slowly and steadily, it can
definitely make you financially strong.
Start small. Start smart. Start early.
And don’t just be a consumer — become an owner.
That’s it for today. See you in the next video. Bye-bye.
